actuation: piston actuation driven by an electric motor
constitutive_assumptions: Silicone rubber is treated as an incompressible, homogeneous Neo-Hookean material
The bending actuator is assumed to deform into the geometry of a torus segment with uniform cross section
The cross-sectional perimeter C and initial cross-sectional area A0 remain constant due to the inextensible strain-limited layer and densely wound fiber reinforcement
Circumferential strain λ2 is assumed to be 1 and the corresponding principal stress σ2 is assumed to be zero
The material incompressibility condition λ1*λ2*λ3 = 1 is assumed, resulting in λ3 = 1/λ1
For small deformation distances dF during stiffness testing, the moment arm length lF is assumed to remain constant
control_variables: In particle diameter tests: braiding angle θ = 130°, wall thickness d0 = 2 mm, hardness H = 5D
In braiding angle tests: particle diameter φ = 2 mm, wall thickness d0 = 2 mm, hardness H = 5D
In wall thickness tests: particle diameter φ = 2 mm, braiding angle θ = 130°, hardness H = 5D
In material hardness tests: particle diameter φ = 2 mm, braiding angle θ = 130°, wall thickness d0 = 2 mm
In medium comparison tests: φ = 2 mm, θ = 130°, d0 = 2 mm, H = 5D
Indenter displacement during rotational stiffness testing fixed at 10 mm
Number of experimental repeats: 30 replicates per volume ratio for stiffness and motion range; 10 repeats for accuracy tests
Silicone mixing ratio fixed at 1:1.01 (EON-A to EON-B) with a 3-hour cure time
dependent_variables: Actuator range of motion / bending angle α
Repeatability / standard deviation of range of motion
Retraction / restoration angle after piston release

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Using particle transmission driven by a motor-actuated piston circumvents fluid-sealing challenges while enabling combined actuation and variable stiffness without bulky pumps or valve manifolds.
Injecting solid particles up to 1.8 times the initial volume produces bending up to 60 degrees and increases rotational stiffness by nearly seven-fold from the unactuated state.

Kinematic bending range and rotational stiffness can be modeled analytically by assuming torus segment expansion and calculating inter-particle contact forces and friction moments from Neo-Hookean membrane tension.
Solid glassy glass balls demonstrated superior performance over stainless steel balls, plastic balls, and beans owing to high hardness, low thermal conductivity, and small friction coefficient.
Smaller particle diameters (2 mm vs. 3 mm and 4 mm) generate a more linear bending response, larger angular deflection, and higher rotational stiffness.

At an injected volume ratio of 1.8, particle transmission generates nearly six-fold greater stiffness and over five-fold greater bending deflection than compressed air, and roughly three-fold higher stiffness than water.

Incomplete elastic restoration occurs after piston retraction due to inter-particle jamming, but embedding miniature vibrators into the strain-limiting layer enables complete recovery to the initial position.

experimental_setup: Silicone rubber bending actuator (EON series) reinforced with double-stranded woven fiberglass thread and molded with 3D-printed PLA molds
Solid glassy glass particles (diameters 2 mm, 3 mm, and 4 mm) driven through a connected cylinder via an electrically driven piston
Test bench equipped with a motorized stage and a force gauge displaced by 10 mm against the actuator endpoint to measure deflection angle, moment arm, and rotational stiffness
Dual-force gauge test bench simultaneously measuring vertical input piston force and horizontal endpoint actuation force
Two 3-finger soft robotic gripper configurations: one with fixed actuator mounting positions and one mounted on a mechanism to enlarge the grasping space for irregularly shaped and heavy tools
Miniature vibration motors embedded in the strain-limiting layer near the cylinder-actuator interface to evaluate recovery dynamics during piston retraction
future_work: Investigating the optimum operating power and vibration frequency of the embedded vibrators for actuator restoration
Further exploring the mechanics of particle chain formation and destruction under granular mechanics principles
independent_variables: Injected particle volume ratio V (from 1.0 to 1.8 in increments of 0.1)
Particle diameter φ (2 mm, 3 mm, 4 mm)
Actuator wall thickness d0 (2 mm, 3 mm, 4 mm)
Transmission medium type (glass particles, unpressurized/pressurized air, unpressurized/pressurized water)
Vibration state during piston retraction (vibrators ON vs. OFF)
limitations_inferred: Analytical model treats deformation as an idealized uniform torus and ignores localized bulging, cylinder wall friction, and dynamic granular packing effects
Integrating rigid electric drive cylinders and vibration motors introduces rigid elements, mass, and wiring that compromise the total compliance and compactness of the soft robotic system
Long-term durability, cyclic fatigue of the silicone membrane, particle wear, and actuation speed/bandwidth were not evaluated
limitations_stated_by_authors: Actuator range of motion reaches an upper limit around a volume ratio of 1.8 where force chains cause particles to behave as a rigid solid, resisting further bending and risking membrane rupture near the inlet
Bending angle of the prototype actuator is relatively small (around 90°), requiring an additional mechanism to grasp large objects
The actuator cannot fully restore to its unactuated baseline without active external vibration due to particle jamming and limited silicone restoring force
Introduced vibration may be undesirable in certain operating environments
Optimal power and frequency for the embedded vibrators were not determined
High stiffness increase may be unsuitable for delicate objects requiring gentle contact, such as eggs
Actuation output force is significantly lower than input piston force because much of the input work is redirected into particle jamming
Motion accuracy and repeatability degrade as injected volume increases (standard deviation increases up to 3° at V = 1.8)
main_results: Increasing injected particle volume from 1.0 to 1.8 times the initial volume enabled the actuator to bend up to 60° (with up to ~90° maximum prototype bending range) and increased rotational stiffness by nearly seven-fold from its unactuated state
Smaller particle size (2 mm) yielded superior linearity, higher angular deflection, and higher rotational stiffness compared to 3 mm and 4 mm particles
Lower braiding angles yielded larger bending motion, whereas braiding angle and wall thickness exhibited minimal impact on rotational stiffness
Lower silicone hardness produced higher rotational stiffness but smaller angular motion at high particle fill levels

Particle transmission achieved roughly 1.5 times higher rotational stiffness than water and twice that of compressed air at equivalent bending angles, while showing nearly six-fold higher stiffness than air and three-fold higher stiffness than water at a volume ratio of 1.8
Output force was lower than input force due to energy dissipation into particle jamming, directly enabling stiffness modulation
Standard deviation of range of motion increased with volume ratio (from 1.8° at V = 1.5 to 3° at V = 1.8)
Embedding vibrators into the strain-limiting layer successfully resolved jamming hysteresis upon piston retraction, achieving complete return to zero angle
modeling_methods: Kinematic volume-expansion modeling linking injected volume ratio to torus-segment bending angle under constant perimeter constraints
Constitutive stress modeling of the silicone unit cell using incompressible Neo-Hookean hyperelastic strain energy and the Young-Laplace equation
Inter-particle contact mechanics modeling normal forces, sliding friction, and resultant resistive friction moments summed across particle layers to determine rotational stiffness
performance_metrics: Bending range of motion / angle α (degrees)
Rotational stiffness SR (FlF / β in N·m/rad or equivalent)
Fold change in rotational stiffness (ratio relative to initial state or fluid baselines)
Input piston force vs. output actuation force (N)
Motion repeatability / standard deviation of bending angle (degrees)
Restoration / retract angle (degrees) with and without vibration
possible_gap_implications: Demonstrates that dry granular materials can act simultaneously as an actuation transmission medium and a variable stiffness mechanism, bypassing the need for fluid seals and pneumatic pumps; however, this single study does not prove general suitability across all soft robotics due to motion range saturation and the necessity of auxiliary vibrators for restoration.
paper.research_objective: To propose, model, fabricate, and experimentally evaluate a novel particle transmission mechanism for soft robotic bending actuators and grippers, enabling simultaneous actuation and multi-fold stiffness modulation via motor-driven piston displacement without requiring strict fluid sealing or pneumatic pumps.
paper.research_problem: Soft robotic actuators traditionally depend on pneumatic or hydraulic transmissions that suffer from sealing difficulties, complex valve arrangements, bulky tethered pumps, and limited ranges of stiffness modulation during grasping.
paper.title: Soft Robotic Grippers Based on Particle Transmission
